content: Glaucoma is a major cause of blindness globally, characterized by progressive loss of peripheral vision and, in advanced stages, central vision, ultimately leading to blindness. Early intervention aims to prevent or delay vision loss. Elevated intraocular pressure (IOP) is the primary modifiable risk factor for glaucoma, typically caused by obstruction of aqueous humor outflow. This can be addressed by either enhancing outflow or reducing aqueous humor production. Cyclodestructive procedures target the ciliary body epithelium, the site of aqueous humor production, to lower IOP. The most common method is laser cyclophotocoagulation. The objective of this study was to evaluate the effectiveness and safety of cyclodestructive procedures for managing non-refractory glaucoma, defined as glaucoma in eyes that have not undergone prior incisional surgery. The study also aimed to compare different laser delivery methods, parameters, and routes of administration in terms of IOP control, visual acuity, pain management, and adverse events. A systematic search was conducted across multiple databases, including CENTRAL, MEDLINE, Embase, LILACS, and ClinicalTrials.gov, up to August 7, 2017. Reference lists of included studies were also reviewed. Only randomized controlled trials (RCTs) comparing cyclophotocoagulation to other interventions or different laser parameters were included. Two reviewers independently screened studies, assessed bias, extracted data, and graded evidence quality according to Cochrane standards. One trial, involving 92 eyes from 92 participants, met the inclusion criteria. This trial evaluated diode transscleral cyclophotocoagulation (TSCPC) as a primary surgical treatment for primary open-angle glaucoma. Conducted in Ghana, the trial compared low-energy (45.0 J) and high-energy (65.5 J) TSCPC, with a mean follow-up of 13.2 months. The trial had a low risk of selection and reporting bias but showed high risk of detection and attrition bias. Thirteen participants with missing follow-up data were excluded, leaving 40 participants in the low-energy group and 39 in the high-energy group for analysis. IOP control, defined as a reduction of at least 20% from baseline, was achieved in 47% of eyes, with similar rates between the lowand high-energy groups. However, the small sample size introduced uncertainty regarding any differences between energy settings (risk ratio [RR] 1.03, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.64 to 1.65; low-certainty evidence). The mean reduction in IOP also showed uncertainty (mean difference [MD] -0.50 mmHg, 95% CI -5.79 to 4.79; low-certainty evidence). Visual acuity outcomes were limited. A decrease in vision, defined as a loss of two or more lines on the Snellen chart or a decline in visual acuity category, occurred in 23% of eyes. The difference between energy groups was uncertain (RR 1.22, 95% CI 0.54 to 2.76; low-certainty evidence). Data on mean visual acuity and changes greater than one line on the Snellen chart were unavailable. The mean number of glaucoma medications used post-treatment was similar between groups (MD 0.10, 95% CI -0.43 to 0.63; moderate-certainty evidence). Retreatment was required in 20% of eyes, but the effect of energy settings on retreatment rates was inconclusive (RR 0.76, 95% CI 0.31 to 1.84; low-certainty evidence). No data were reported on visual field outcomes, cost-effectiveness, or quality of life. Adverse events were reported for the entire study population rather than by treatment group. Most participants experienced mild to moderate pain and transient conjunctival burns. Severe iritis occurred in two eyes, and hyphema was observed in three eyes. No cases of hypotony or phthisis bulbi were reported. The only adverse event reported by treatment group was atonic pupil, with no significant difference between groups (RR 0.89, 95% CI 0.47 to 1.68; low-certainty evidence). In conclusion, there is insufficient evidence to determine the relative effectiveness and safety of cyclodestructive procedures for the primary management of non-refractory glaucoma. The single included trial did not compare cyclophotocoagulation to other procedural interventions and provided uncertain results regarding differences between lowand high-energy TSCPC. The overall effect of laser treatment on IOP control was modest, and the incidence of vision loss was limited. Further research is needed to address the management of non-refractory glaucoma.
